6.  **★★★ Attacking your own watermark (bonus).** After lab 2: paraphrase the marked texts (via an LLM, instruction "rewrite with the same ideas"), measure the drop in $z$ as a function of the rate of replaced tokens, and estimate the rate needed to fall below $z = 2$. Conclude on the sentence "a watermark is a marker, not a proof".

    ::: proof
    Guidance: each change that turns one green token red lowers $s_G$ by one, hence $z$ by $1/\sqrt{T\gamma(1-\gamma)}$ (prop. 10.2).

    A token replaced at random was green with probability $p_\delta$ and is green with probability $\gamma$ afterwards, so it lowers $\mathbb E[z]$ by about $(p_\delta - \gamma)/\sqrt{T\gamma(1-\gamma)}$ at its own position — and by as much again at the next position, whose green list it reseeds.

    Going from $\mathbb E[z] = 7$ to 2 means leaving only $2/7$ of the positions marked. With the hash of the previous token, a position stays marked only if neither it nor its predecessor was replaced, with probability $(1-\rho)^2$ for a replacement rate $\rho$: hence $\rho \approx 1 - \sqrt{2/7} \approx 0.47$, nearly half of the tokens — the text that survives the attack is so transformed that *content* traceability (plagiarism) becomes the issue again, not that of *the machine*. Loop closed with ch. 10. [∎]{.qed}
    :::

## Projects and assessment {#projects}

The official assessment, from the fiche: not displayed — the 2026–2027 SynapseS catalogue has published no course description for this module (its S3 and S4 tracks are empty), so no modality, weight or exam is given. Everything below is therefore a proposal: one project, solo or in a group, assessed on a report and a talk, and a written exam for a final or resit session.

The projects exercise objectives O2 (generative modelling theory: the bias of masking, CFG and exponential tilting), O3 (LLMs: constrained decoding, steering, RLHF and DPO, watermarking) and O8 (trustworthy AI: provenance, attacks, robustness budgets), with O7 through the labs and O4–O5 through the graph generators of ch. 8. Exercise 1 (the automaton mask as a `LogitsProcessor`) is reused by the Year 2 transverse projects [Y2.2](../../projects/index.html#y2-2), [Y2.4](../../projects/index.html#y2-4) and [Y2.5](../../projects/index.html#y2-5) of the [projects page](../../projects/index.html), and the second group project below feeds Y2.4.

### Solo projects {#projects-solo}

1.  **[Solo · ≈ 25 h] Paper study: "A Watermark for Large Language Models" (Kirchenbauer, Geiping, Wen, Katz, Miers & Goldstein, ICML 2023).** Does the z-test keep its power on a small open model, how many edits erase the mark, and what does the mark cost in text quality?
    -   *Implement*: the green/red scheme (definition 6.1) and the unigram variant (Zhao et al., 2023) as `LogitsProcessor`s; the z-test (theorem 6.2); three attacks — synonym swaps, homoglyphs, paraphrase by a small instruction model.
    -   *Data*: prompts from the "realnewslike" split of C4, as in the paper; OPT-1.3B or a smaller open model on a free GPU; the human continuations of the same documents as the null sample.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. *Chapters*: ch. 6, ch. 9, ch. 10.
    -   *Success*: power curves against $T$, $\gamma$ and $\delta$ with intervals; no false positive at $z > 4$ on at least 1,000 human texts; the drop of $z$ against the edit rate compared with the prediction of exercise 6; the perplexity cost measured under a larger model.
2.  **[Solo · ≈ 25 h] Prompt, steering or DPO: three ways to impose a formal register.** At an equal quality budget, which control buys the most formality for the least loss of diversity?
    -   *Implement*: prompting (conditioning); contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et al., ACL 2024, published under the name Rimsky) with a vector from formal/informal sentence pairs (ch. 4); a small DPO fine-tune with LoRA (proposition 5.3) on pairs ranked by a formality classifier; a sweep of each strength — prompt variants, $\alpha$, $1/\beta$.
    -   *Data*: news articles of CNN/DailyMail to summarize; the sentence-level formality ratings of Pavlick & Tetreault (TACL 2016) for the contrast pairs and the classifier; Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. *Chapters*: ch. 4, ch. 5, ch. 9.
    -   *Success*: the three fidelity/diversity curves of proposition 9.3 on the same axes, with bootstrap intervals over 3 seeds; ROUGE against the reference summaries reported as the quality budget; the elbow of each method named and justified.
3.  **[Solo · ≈ 25 h] Paper study: "Null-text Inversion for Editing Real Images using Guided Diffusion Models" (Mokady, Hertz, Aberman, Pritch & Cohen-Or, CVPR 2023).** How much of the drift of DDIM inversion under guidance does null-text optimization remove, and how many inner steps does it need?
    -   *Implement*: DDIM inversion with $w = 1$ and regeneration at $w = 7.5$, to exhibit the drift (proposition 7.3); null-text optimization (definition 7.4), with the gradient through the unconditional branch only; one Prompt-to-Prompt word swap.
    -   *Data*: Stable Diffusion v1.4, the model of the paper, through the diffusers library, in half precision on a free 16 GB GPU; 20 captioned images of COCO 2017 validation.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. *Chapters*: ch. 7, ch. 9.
    -   *Success*: PSNR and LPIPS of the reconstruction for 0, 1, 5 and 10 inner steps, with intervals over the 20 images, against plain inversion at $w = 7.5$; three edits shown with their failure cases.

### Group projects {#projects-group}

1.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] How biased is masked decoding?** On languages small enough to enumerate, how far is the masked law from the true conditional, and what does it cost to correct it?
    -   *Implement*: the mask of ch. 3 as a `LogitsProcessor` (exercise 1); the exact law $p_\theta(\cdot \mid S)$ by scoring every element of $S$; the masked law from the per-step masses $Z_t$ (proposition 2.2); rejection (proposition 2.4); sequential Monte Carlo with particles weighted by $\prod_t Z_t$ (Lew et al., 2023); grammar-aligned decoding (Park, Wang, Berg-Kirkpatrick, Polikarpova & D'Antoni, NeurIPS 2024) as the paper study.
    -   *Data*: three finite languages — the 366 dates of 2024 written DD/MM/YYYY, a list of 200 country names, the calls of a two-field JSON schema with enumerated values (example 3.5); GPT-2 and Qwen2.5-0.5B on a laptop CPU.
    -   *Split*: one member on the automata and the exact enumeration; one on rejection, SMC and grammar-aligned decoding; one on the evaluation (KL, validity, diversity of ch. 9).
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 6–8 page report, a 15-minute talk. *Chapters*: ch. 2, ch. 3, ch. 9. The same question for valence masks continues in [Graph Generative Models, ch. 3](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html#ch3).
    -   *Success*: the exact divergence between the conditional and the masked law for each language and model; every measured ratio inside the band of proposition 2.2 for the observed $\varepsilon$; the divergence of SMC against the number of particles, at a counted number of forward passes.
2.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] Secure structured tool calls: a grammar-constrained agent under prompt injection.** A mask guarantees valid calls; does it reduce, leave unchanged or hide the success of injections that stay syntactically valid?
    -   *Implement*: an agent whose tool calls are constrained by their JSON schemas (example 3.5, with Outlines, XGrammar or the mask of exercise 1); indirect injections that keep every call valid (theorem 10.1); a probe of grammar complexity (compile time and states against nesting and enumerations); three defenses — semantic validation of arguments, least-privilege tools, spotlighting of untrusted content.
    -   *Data*: the AgentDojo benchmark (Debenedetti et al., NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks), its banking and workspace suites; a small open instruction model with tool calling.
    -   *Split*: the constrained tool layer; the red team (injections and complexity probe); the defenses and the evaluation.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 6–8 page report, a 15-minute talk. *Chapters*: ch. 3, ch. 10. Builds on [Large Language Models, 9.4](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#attacks) and its agents of ch. 8; feeds the dispatcher project Y2.4.
    -   *Success*: utility and attack success rate without the mask, with it, then with each defense, with intervals over the tasks; the share of successful attacks whose calls were valid; a measured blow-up of states or compile time, and the limit that stops it.
3.  **[Group of 4 · ≈ 30 h each] One control curve, three modalities.** Does one protocol — strength sweep, fidelity/diversity curve, robustness budget — describe guidance on images, text and molecules, and where does the analogy break?
    -   *Implement*: a CFG sweep on a small class-conditional diffusion model trained with condition dropout (ch. 7); a steering sweep on GPT-2 (ch. 4); a conditional SMILES language model trained with a property-bin token dropped 10% of the time, guided in logit space as in example 7.5 (ch. 8); the protocol of proposition 9.3 and the budget of definition 10.3, under one attack per modality.
    -   *Data*: Fashion-MNIST, its classes as conditions; the prompts of example 4.2; ZINC250k, with RDKit for QED and validity.
    -   *Split*: one member per modality; one on the shared harness (fidelity, diversity, precision and recall, attacks).
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 6–8 page report, a 15-minute talk. *Chapters*: ch. 4, ch. 7, ch. 8, ch. 9, ch. 10. Connects [Multimodal GenAI, ch. 4](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html#ch4) and [Graph Generative Models, ch. 7](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html#ch7).
    -   *Success*: the three curves on normalized axes with intervals over 3 seeds; the elbow of each; at least one place where the single-step prediction of exercise 4 fails, explained.

### Written exam (proposal) {#projects-exam}

Format: 2 hours, one handwritten A4 sheet of notes allowed, no electronic device; four questions, 20 points.

1.  **Question (4 points).** For each mechanism, give its family (definition 2.1), its guarantee and its main cost: (a) a JSON-schema mask on tool calls; (b) CFG with $w = 5$; (c) resampling until a validator accepts; (d) a green/red watermark. Then say when you choose a hard constraint rather than guidance. *Expected*:
    -   (a) hard constraint: validity by construction, one pass plus a mask, and a law renormalized step by step, hence biased (proposition 2.2);
    -   (b) guidance: statistical fidelity, two network passes per step, diversity lost as $w$ grows (ch. 9);
    -   (c) post-processing: the exact conditional law, at an expected $1/p_\theta(S \mid x)$ draws (proposition 2.4);
    -   (d) guidance used for provenance: a statistical test, a quality cost that grows with $\delta$.
    -   A hard constraint when a failure is catastrophic (a parser, a valence), guidance when it is gradual (tone, style).
2.  **Question (6 points).** A green/red watermark uses $\gamma = 0.25$.
    -   (a) A text of 400 tokens contains 150 green tokens: compute $z$ and conclude at the threshold $z = 4$.
    -   (b) How many green tokens must an attacker exchange for red ones to bring $z$ below 4? Assume that each exchange lowers $s_G$ by exactly one.
    -   (c) With the exponential-minimum scheme instead, another text of 400 tokens has score 480. Conclude, first with a normal approximation of the null law, then with its exact tail, about $8 \times 10^{-5}$.

    *Expected*:
    -   (a) the standard deviation is $\sqrt{400 \cdot 0.25 \cdot 0.75} = \sqrt{75} \approx 8.66$, so $z = 50 / 8.66 \approx 5.77 > 4$: reject H0 (one-sided $p$-value $\approx 4 \times 10^{-9}$).
    -   (b) each exchange lowers $z$ by $1/8.66 \approx 0.115$; $z < 4$ requires $s_G < 134.6$, so $s_G \leq 134$: 16 exchanges.
    -   (c) under H0 the score is $\mathrm{Gamma}(400, 1)$, of mean 400 and standard deviation 20, so the normal approximation gives $z = 4$, just at the threshold. The exact tail is larger than the normal one ($3 \times 10^{-5}$): at that level, do not accuse.
3.  **Question (5 points).** Masking at each step the tokens that make a set $S$ unreachable.
    -   (a) Show on an example that it does not sample the conditional law $p_\theta(\cdot \mid x, S)$.
    -   (b) Prove that if every output of $S$ has at most $T$ steps and the mask never removes more than a mass $\varepsilon$, the masked law is within a factor $(1-\varepsilon)^{\pm T}$ of the conditional one.

    *Expected*:
    -   (a) the two-token example 2.3: the masked law gives $aa$ the probability $0.5$, the conditional law $0.05/0.55 \approx 0.09$.
    -   (b) on $S$ the masked law is the model's law divided by $\prod_t Z_t$, so the ratio is $p_\theta(S \mid x) / \prod_t Z_t$.
    -   Each $Z_t$ lies in $[1-\varepsilon, 1]$, so the product over at most $T$ steps lies in $[(1-\varepsilon)^T, 1]$, and $p_\theta(S \mid x)$ is an average of such products under the masked law: the ratio lies in the band.
4.  **Question (5 points).** Let the numbers $r_v$, one per token of the vocabulary, be i.i.d. uniform on $[0, 1]$, and let $p$ be a law on the vocabulary. Prove that $y = \arg\max_v r_v^{1/p_v}$ has law $p$. Then give the null law of the detection score of proposition 6.4 over $T$ tokens.

    *Expected*:
    -   $E_v = -\log r_v$ are i.i.d. exponential of rate 1, and maximizing $r_v^{1/p_v}$ is minimizing $E_v / p_v$, exponential of rate $p_v$.
    -   The minimum of independent exponentials is reached at $v$ with probability $p_v / \sum_u p_u = p_v$: no distortion at each step.
    -   Under H0 the text ignores the key, each $r_{y_t}$ is uniform, each term is $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$, and the sum is $\mathrm{Gamma}(T, 1)$: mean $T$, variance $T$.

### Grading rubric (proposal) {#projects-rubric}

| Criterion | Weight | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Problem formulation | 15 % | the control written on the grid of ch. 2: family, admissible set or target, strength parameter; assumptions stated |
| Correct implementation | 25 % | masks, guidance and tests checked first on a case with a known answer (an enumerable language, a toy law, a null sample) |
| Experimental rigour | 25 % | strength sweeps with fixed seeds, fidelity and diversity reported together, baselines at an equal compute budget, intervals |
| Link to the theory | 15 % | which result of the course (proposition 2.2, theorem 6.2, theorem 7.1, theorem 9.2) predicts what, and whether the measurement agrees |
| Robustness and honesty | 10 % | at least one attack or failure case reported (ch. 10); negative results kept |
| Communication and reproducibility | 10 % | clear report and talk; one command reproduces the main figure |
